title: Swing voters, economic worries drive decisive blue wave in U.S. midterms

 Adrian Morrow U.S. Correspondent Nathan VanderKlippe International correspondent Washington and columbus, ohio Published 3 hours ago Updated 1 hour ago Open this photo in gallery: U.S. President Donald Trump talks to reporters during a tour of the White House ballroom, still under construction, on Wednesday. Alex Brandon/The Associated Press 
 Comments Share Save for later Please log in to bookmark this story. Log In Create an account As the dust settled on the Democratic Party’s landslide victory in U.S. midterm elections, the scale of the blowout came into sharper focus – as did the key groups of voters who delivered President Donald Trump a thundering rebuke and the reasons for their anger.
 The Democrats’ popular-vote margin in the U.S. House of Representatives was the highest in any election since 1976, with the Republicans routed across several of their strongholds, from Texas to South Carolina to Kansas.
 Latinos and young voters swung sharply away from Mr. Trump, while Black Americans turned out in disproportionately high numbers, particularly across the South.
 Andrew Coyne: U.S. midterms are a rebuke to the Republicans, but not the wipeout they deserved 
 Economic anxiety, particularly frustration with consumer inflation driven by Mr. Trump’s war on Iran and global tariffs, was the election’s dominant issue. But there are signs that the President’s violent and often deadly immigration crackdown and accusations of corruption also played a part in the backlash.
 Mr. Trump seemed uninterested in discussing his party’s bloodbath during a public appearance on Wednesday. He spent more than 20 minutes touring reporters through his under-construction White House ballroom and touting various other Washington building projects, including a triumphal arch and a golf course.
 The Associated Press 
 Asked about the election, he said it was “largely true” that frustration with the Iran war caused the Republican defeat “because it drove the gasoline up a little bit short term” when Tehran blockaded the Strait of Hormuz.
 “At the same time, if I had to do it again, I’d have to do it again,” he said. “You can’t let Iran have a nuclear weapon.”
 In an era of divided politics and tight electoral margins, the Democratic victory was surprisingly decisive. The party is on track to win the popular vote for the House by 13 percentage points. By comparison, the Democratic margin in 2018 was a little under nine and the Republican one in 2010 was 6.6. 
 David Shribman: Americans spoke loudly in the midterms, but time will tell whether they were a turning point 
 Democrats have secured at least 237 of 435 House districts, their best result since 2008, with dozens of races still to be called. They will hold at least 54 seats in the Senate, with counting continuing in both Mississippi and Alaska.
 More stunning than the size of the new Democratic majorities was where they were won. Texas, which Mr. Trump handily carried three times and where no Democrat has prevailed in a Senate contest since 1988, sent James Talarico to the chamber by a 12-point margin.
 Adam Hamilton became the first Democrat to win a Senate race in Kansas since 1932 while South Carolina, which Mr. Trump took just two years ago by 18 points, chose Annie Andrews over Darline Graham, the sister of the state’s long-time Republican senator. 
 The Associated Press 
 Other red-state Senate-seat pickups for the Democrats included Ohio and Iowa. The party also flipped Republican upper-chamber seats in North Carolina, a swing state, and Maine, which is predominantly blue.
 Democratic gains in the House stretched from the populous swing state of Pennsylvania to reliably red Kentucky, Iowa and Texas. The party took governors’ mansions away from the Republicans in Texas, Georgia, Ohio, Iowa and Nevada.
 Mr. Trump solidified his 2024 return to the White House by making inroads with young men and Latinos. This time, both groups moved resoundingly to the Democrats.
 Polling by the New York Times showed a 17-percentage-point swing away from the Republicans among men, along with a 32-point swing for voters between 18 and 29 years of age. NBC’s exit polling showed the Democrats winning nearly three-quarters of voters in this age group.
 Latino voters, according to the Times’ data, voted 69 per cent for the Democrats, a 28-point swing from two years ago. They said they trusted Democrats more on the issue of immigration than Republicans by a 27-point margin. The group has been the primary target of the President’s campaign of roundups and deportations.
 Six takeaways from Democrats’ resounding midterm sweep 
 The effect of this was particularly clear in Texas: Mr. Trump won Hidalgo County, with its overwhelmingly Latino population along the Mexican border, in 2024; this week, it gave Mr. Talarico more than 72 per cent of its vote.
 Turnout among Black voters in much of the South, meanwhile, was high. This voting demographic is consistently the Democrats’ most loyal.
 An Associated Press survey put election participation among voters in DeKalb County, a majority-Black part of the Atlanta suburbs, for instance, at 86 per cent of 2024 levels, unusually elevated for a non-presidential race. Georgia Democratic Senator Jon Ossoff won re-election by 18 percentage points.
 Reuters 
 It was a similar story in Mississippi, where 89 per cent of 2024 voters in the county that contains the state capital, Jackson, also cast ballots this week. The vote count in the state is virtually tied between incumbent Senator Cindy Hyde-Smith and Democratic challenger Scott Colom.
 The AP also found that two-thirds of midterm voters believed Mr. Trump’s policies had made the economy worse, amid persistently high gas and grocery prices. In addition to petroleum, the Hormuz blockade has cut global fertilizer supplies.
 Scott Elisar, an Ohio lawyer who joined a cheering crowd at the Democratic Party’s election night event in Columbus, said the midterm vote was “a rejection of a war that makes no sense to people, of gas prices that are $4.40 a gallon and make no sense to people.”
 Mr. Trump’s protectionist trade policies, which have entailed imposing tariffs on nearly every country in the world, have also saddled American consumers with billions of dollars in additional costs.
 Willie Mitchell, a 56-year-old bus driver in the Detroit suburbs, described the President’s trade war on Canada as “the dumbest thing ever” as it led to shifts being cut at Michigan auto plants.
 “It hurts a state like this because we have such close relations. We do a lot of trading back and forth,” he said.
 In the AP poll, half of respondents cited government corruption as important to their midterm vote – a result that could reflect growing public anger over accusations that Mr. Trump and his family have used the presidency to enrich themselves.
 Successful Democratic candidates spanned the party’s ideological spectrum from centrists to socialists, but many of them adopted rhetoric seemingly inspired by leftist Vermont Senator Bernie Sanders, tying a message of economic populism to criticism of a corrupt elite.
 “While the wealthy and well-lobbied feast on inside information and official favours, America’s forgotten families are treated to systemic corporate disrespect and official indifference,” warned Mr. Ossoff in his victory speech.
 Mike Nellis, an Illinois Democratic strategist, said the result showed that campaigning on issues such as “class, the economy and taking on entrenched power” is “the magic secret sauce.”
 The seven Democratic Senate candidates who won seats previously occupied by Republicans also represent generational change: they are, on average, nearly a decade younger than the average among sitting U.S. senators.
